findings.title: Findings converge on the synthetic state event
findings.why_it_matters: Both HIGH findings come from the same place: `make_synthetic_state_event` builds an event that doesn't look like a real one, and the fact that it is synthetic lives on the `InvokeHandler` command (`cmd.is_synthetic`), not on the event. Its topic carries an entity suffix that real events never carry (Finding 2), and its context id is a fresh `uuid4()` with origin `LOCAL` (Finding 3). Today one consumer copes, because `build_execution_record` holds the command and special-cases it. This design adds two consumers that only hold the event: the new extraction function's topic field, and the predicate-error path. #1817's near-miss rows will add a third. Each finding's local fix teaches one more consumer to work around the synthetic shape: normalize the topic here, thread an `is_synthetic` flag there. Should the synthetic event's representation be re-evaluated before patching each consumer? Re-evaluation includes leaving the event as it is and accepting the consumer-side handling.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate the synthetic state event before addressing Findings 2 and 3 individually. Open questions: should a synthetic event be distinguishable from the event alone, and by what? Should its topic match a real event's? Does a fabricated context id need to exist at all? Do the consumers of `cmd.is_synthetic` still need it afterwards?
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate the synthetic state event before addressing Findings 2 and 3 individually.
findings.choice_reason: Re-evaluation settled: build the synthetic event from the cached state's real context and base topic, keep the command-side HASSETTE_SYNTHETIC label (ledger D7)

findings.title: D3's `event.topic` has two shapes for the same trigger, and its "names users subscribe with" rationale doesn't hold
findings.why_it_matters: A real Home Assistant `state_changed` event has `topic="hass.event.state_changed"`, the bare base topic. The per-entity and domain-wildcard topics exist only as routes built in `expand_topics`. The synthetic immediate-fire event carries `hass.event.state_changed.<entity_id>`. So `trigger_topic` holds two shapes for the same kind of trigger, and a query like `WHERE trigger_topic = 'hass.event.state_changed'`, or grouping by topic, silently drops every immediate-fire row. D3 was ratified on "never empty, same names users subscribe with". The first half holds. The second doesn't: an `on_state_change("light.office")` user subscribes at the entity route, and the real row would store the base topic.
findings.recommended: A: Keep `event.topic` as the event-kind field. Make every row store the base topic (normalize the synthetic event, or derive it from the payload), and reword D3's rationale to "event kind, filled for every run".
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Predicate-error rows on synthetic events would record a fabricated context id and origin
findings.why_it_matters: D5 says predicate-error rows "record the event's real context id and origin". The immediate-fire path and the duration fire-time recheck both evaluate predicates against a synthetic event, which has context `id=str(uuid4())` and origin `"LOCAL"`. When a `where=` predicate raises there, `record_predicate_failure` gets only that event. The extraction function can't tell it's synthetic, because the marker lives on `cmd.is_synthetic`, which this path doesn't have. The row would carry a random UUID as `trigger_context_id`, origin `LOCAL`, and a parent id. That is the dishonest context D5 keeps off normal synthetic rows, and anyone tracing that id in the HA logbook hits a dead end that looks real.
findings.recommended: A: Put the synthetic marker on the event, so the extractor emits NULL context and parent id and `HASSETTE_SYNTHETIC` origin whenever it holds a synthetic event.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: D6 leaves `hassette execution`'s not-found and partial-failure behavior unspecified
findings.why_it_matters: D6's table says human mode reads "execution record not found" with logs still shown. It doesn't say what `--json` holds then (`"execution": null`, a missing key, or an error exit), what the exit code is, or what happens when one of the two calls fails (for example a telemetry 503) while the other succeeds. Execution rows are written through `enqueue_record` and a batch drain. Someone who sees an error and runs the command right away can land inside the flush window, and "not found" then reads as "retained away", which sends Claude-driven troubleshooting, the stated `--json` consumer, the wrong way. #3677 adds keys to the same object, so the contract needs pinning now.
findings.recommended: A: Lenient contract as in the table. Document it in `docs/pages/cli/commands.md`, and update `tests/unit/cli/test_commands_log.py` and `tests/snapshots/cli_help.txt` if help text changes.
findings.chosen: A: Lenient contract as in the table.

findings.title: The PR's three breaking changes need named compat entries and one `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer covering all of them
findings.why_it_matters: D1's table says compat ignore entries are "Likely" but doesn't name them, and the Posture section mentions the ignore files but not the footer. The PR carries three breaks: D1 removes `Execution.trigger_context_id`/`trigger_origin`, D4 renames the `hassette.bus` export `DurationConfig` (and `Listener.duration_config`), and D6 changes `hassette execution --json` from a list to an object. CLAUDE.md says the squash-merged PR title becomes the changelog line and release-please keeps only the first footer, so D4's separate `refactor:` commit title never reaches the changelog. The one footer has to name all three breaks. The D1 break is silent for released clients: an upgraded server sends no flat fields, and the old client model defaults them to `None`, which looks the same as "no context". That consequence belongs in the footer.
findings.chosen: In `## Build`, add checkpoints: run `check_wire_compat` and `uv run nox -s client_compat`, and add each line they print to the matching ignore file with a reason comment. State that the PR title uses `feat!:` and the PR body ends with exactly one `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer naming (1) the removed flat `Execution` trigger fields, which released clients now read as `None`, (2) `DurationConfig` → `EntityWatch` and `Listener.duration_config` → `Listener.entity_watch`, and (3) `hassette execution --json` returning an object. Point D4's "changelog line" at this footer.

findings.title: The `DurationConfig` rename breaks an mkdocs autoref the Docs list doesn't cover
findings.why_it_matters: `docs/pages/core-concepts/internals/service-details.md:69` links `[DurationConfig][hassette.bus.listeners.DurationConfig]` and describes it as "Duration-hold configuration and timer lifecycle". After D4's rename the autoref dangles, which fails a strict docs build, and the description no longer fits. The Summary's Docs bullet lists only the CLI and telemetry pages.
findings.chosen: Add `docs/pages/core-concepts/internals/service-details.md` to the Docs bullet in the Summary: retarget the autoref to `hassette.bus.listeners.EntityWatch` and describe it as the listener's entity-tracking config (entity, tracked attribute, duration hold).

findings.title: D4 doesn't say that `_duration_configs_match` compares the new `attribute` field
findings.why_it_matters: `Listener.config_matches()`/`diff_fields()` use `_duration_configs_match`, which compares `is_attribute_listener`. D4 makes that bool a property derived from `attribute`, so the existing comparison still compiles but keeps comparing a bool. Two attribute listeners on the same entity that track different attributes would compare equal on this field. In practice `build_attr_preds` puts the attribute into the predicate, which is compared separately, so behavior is likely unchanged. But the docstring would misdescribe the compared fields, and the config's own field would go unchecked.
findings.chosen: In D4, state that `_duration_configs_match` (and its docstring) compares `attribute` in place of `is_attribute_listener`. Add a unit test in `tests/unit/bus/test_listeners.py` showing that two configs differing only in `attribute` don't match.

findings.title: D2's display-string rules leave escaping, null-versus-missing and the cut unit open
findings.why_it_matters: `json.dumps` defaults to `ensure_ascii=True`, so a non-ASCII attribute (a friendly name in `source_list`) expands to `\uXXXX`, six characters per character. The 255 cap then cuts the escaped text, possibly mid-escape, and the result is unreadable. A JSON-null attribute dumps to `"null"`, while a missing attribute stores NULL per the Assumed section, and the design never says these differ. A value that isn't JSON-serializable raises inside the never-raise path and nulls every field, not just that one.
findings.chosen: Add to D2's ratified storage rule: non-string values use `json.dumps(value, ensure_ascii=False, separators=(",", ":"), default=str)`. A missing state or attribute stores NULL, while an explicit JSON `null` stores `"null"`. The 255 limit counts code points of the stored string, with the `…` included. The remaining ambiguities (`21.5` vs `"21.5"`, a real trailing `…`) are already accepted under "values are for reading".

findings.title: The design doesn't say what a state-change row records for a listener without an `EntityWatch`
findings.why_it_matters: A `DurationConfig`/`EntityWatch` is built only when an `entity_id` is passed (`bus.py:691-700`). A raw `bus.on(topic="hass.event.state_changed.*")` listener has none. The Assumed section's "the `state` key, or the tracked attribute" presumes a watch. Wildcard listeners are the issue's stated motivation, so the extractor's rule for them should be explicit.
findings.chosen: Reword the Assumed bullet on old and new values: any event with a `RawStateChangePayload` records the `state` values, unless the listener's `EntityWatch.attribute` is set, in which case it records that attribute's values. A listener with no `EntityWatch` records state values.

findings.title: Duration rows record the event that started the hold, not the state at fire time
findings.why_it_matters: A duration listener's `invoke_fn` closes over the event that started the hold. The fire-time recheck builds a throwaway synthetic event that is used only for `hold_matches` and never reaches the record. The recorded `new_value` is therefore the value from N seconds before `execution_start_ts`, and attributes may have changed in between. That arguably answers "what fired it", and it's exactly the event the handler received. It will still surprise a user comparing the row to current state, and the design doesn't say which one it records.
findings.recommended: A: Record the event that started the hold, and add one sentence to `docs/pages/core-concepts/database-telemetry.md` saying duration and debounced rows show the triggering event, not the state at fire time.
findings.chosen: A: Record the event that started the hold, and add one sentence to `docs/pages/core-concepts/database-telemetry.md` saying duration and debounced rows show the triggering event, not the state at fire time.

findings.title: Extraction failures are logged only at DEBUG, so a payload-shape change silently blanks every row
findings.why_it_matters: The extraction function "never raises: any failure leaves the fields NULL and logs at DEBUG". A NULL entity is already a normal value (`call_service` events, Hassette events), so after an HA payload change every row degrades to blank trigger fields with nothing at the default log level. That's a dark operation under `logging.md`: an `except` that doesn't re-raise must log at a level someone will see. The same file already logs recorder failures with `logger.exception`. The failure is also all-or-nothing: one bad value nulls fields that would have extracted fine.
findings.recommended: A: Log extraction failures with `logger.exception` (WARNING-level visibility) and keep the fields NULL. Don't log values (see Finding 12).
findings.chosen: A: Log extraction failures with `logger.exception` (WARNING-level visibility) and keep the fields NULL. Don't log values (see Finding 12).

findings.title: Tracked attribute and state values are stored as Home Assistant reports them, with no redaction
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a deployment where the web API or the DB file is reachable by someone other than the HA owner. D2's 255-character cut is a size bound, not a privacy bound. Attributes such as `entity_picture` (signed token URLs), `access_token`, or `device_tracker` latitude/longitude would be written to hassette's SQLite file and served through `/api/telemetry/execution/{id}` and `hassette execution --json`. HA already holds these values, but hassette's DB and API didn't before.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: tracked values are stored as Home Assistant reports them, stated in `database-telemetry.md` and the Posture section.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: tracked values are stored as Home Assistant reports them, stated in `database-telemetry.md` and the Posture section.

findings.title: Nothing records that `hassette execution --json` has no known list-parsing consumer
findings.why_it_matters: D6 ratified the list-to-object break. The ledger doesn't record any check that something parses the list. The critic found no in-repo script or skill that does. Docs (`log-identity.md:33`, `workflows.md`) mention the command but don't parse its JSON. CLAUDE.md's framework rule says in-repo absence isn't evidence of no demand, so the check only measures blast radius.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: an external script parsing `hassette execution --json` as a list breaks, as D6 already accepts.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: an external script parsing `hassette execution --json` as a list breaks, as D6 already accepts.

findings.title: `tools/client_compat_live_state.py:417` constructs executions with the flat fields and is missing from D1's file list
D7's "only unlabelled case" is wrong: a raising hold predicate at the duration fire-time recheck also writes an unlabelled synthetic row
findings.why_it_matters: D7 says "The only unlabelled case is a raising `where=` during an immediate fire". D8 says the recheck's synthetic event "never reaches the record". Neither holds. `on_duration_fire` builds `recheck_event = self.make_synthetic_event(...)` and calls `hold_matches`, which goes through `evaluate_predicate`. A raise there calls `record_predicate_failure` (wired to `BusService.record_predicate_failure_safely`), and that calls `summarize_trigger(event, listener, is_synthetic=False)`. The result is an error row with origin `LOCAL`, old value NULL, new value equal to the cached state at fire time, and the context of whichever change last set that state. It looks like an ordinary Home Assistant change, but it describes a hassette-built event, and D8 says duration rows describe the event that started the hold. Before this change these rows had no trigger fields. Now their fields look plausible and are wrong, on the row a user reads to debug a broken predicate.
findings.recommended: A: Pass `is_synthetic=True` from the two synthetic call sites through `evaluate_predicate`/`record_predicate_failure` into `summarize_trigger`, and add a test for the recheck failure row. Correct the D7 and D8 text to match.
findings.chosen: A: Thread is_synthetic through predicate failure

findings.title: No end-to-end test pins D7's handler-visible event or the persisted immediate-fire row, and the existing structure test's docstring is stale
findings.why_it_matters: D7 changes what user handlers observe on immediate fires: `event.topic` becomes the base `hass.event.state_changed`, and `event.payload.context` becomes the cached state's real context. It also changes the persisted row, which keeps the real context, NULL old value and `HASSETTE_SYNTHETIC` origin. Only the factory (`test_synthetic_event_carries_cached_context_and_base_topic`) and `build_execution_record` are unit-tested. `test_immediate_synthetic_event_structure` asserts neither the topic nor that the context matches the seeded state. Its docstring still says "unique context.id" and it asserts `parent_id is None`, both of which reflect the old uuid4 behaviour. A regression in the wiring (`listener.topic` as route at `build_tracked_invoke_fn`, `is_synthetic=True`, the builder re-nulling context) would pass the suite.
findings.chosen: pin D7 end to end in the immediate-fire integration test

findings.title: The planned BREAKING CHANGE footer omits the handler-visible change to `event.topic` and `event.payload.context` on immediate fires
findings.why_it_matters: D7 knowingly accepted that handlers now see a base-topic `event.topic` and a real `event.payload.context` on immediate fires and duration rechecks. The Build checklist's footer item names three breaks: the flat wire fields, `DurationConfig` → `EntityWatch`, and the `--json` shape. It does not name this one, which is the only change that alters what running user code receives. A user app that parses the entity from `event.topic.rsplit(".", 1)[-1]` in an immediate-fire handler, or that treats `context.id` as unique per fire, breaks silently. No bus docs page describes the immediate-fire event's shape either.
findings.recommended: A: Add item (4) to design.md's footer checklist: on `immediate=True` fires and duration rechecks, `event.topic` is now `hass.event.state_changed` (no entity suffix) and `event.payload.context` is the cached state's real context. Add one sentence to the `immediate=` docs.
findings.chosen: B: Keep the footer at three items

findings.title: `make_synthetic_state_event` now hard-indexes `current_state["context"]`; a context-less cached state disables immediate fire and drops a duration recheck
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: open-source library with unknown test callers. The old factory read nothing from the cached state but `new_state` and used a fresh uuid4. The new one raises `KeyError` if the cached dict lacks `context`. In `immediate_fire_task` the broad `except` turns that into a WARNING ("immediate fire will not occur"), and the listener never fires. In `on_duration_fire` there is only a `finally`, so the exception escapes the timer callback and the fire is dropped. A field the predicate doesn't need has made a total function partial.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a cached state without `context` (impossible from HA or the testing factories) skips that listener's immediate fire with a WARNING and drops the duration recheck.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a cached state without `context` (impossible from HA or the testing factories) skips that listener's immediate fire with a WARNING and drops the duration recheck.

findings.title: A payload-shape break logs one full traceback per listener per event into the same database
findings.why_it_matters: The Posture says extraction failures log "once per failing event". The Build changed this to once per row, because the summary is built per `InvokeHandler` and deduplicating across listeners would need per-event shared state. That reason holds. The cost it didn't weigh: one broken payload shape seen by N matching listeners writes N `LOGGER.exception` tracebacks per event, and log records persist to `log_records` in the same SQLite database the executions go to. An HA or hassette release that breaks extraction for every state change would produce a sustained burst of traceback writes at startup of the bad upgrade. The Posture text is also now stale against the code.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: if a payload change breaks extraction for every event, each matching listener's run logs its own traceback. Update the Posture wording to "once per failed row".
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: if a payload change breaks extraction for every event, each matching listener's run logs its own traceback. Update the Posture wording to "once per failed row".

findings.title: Value truncation serializes the full value before slicing, on the dispatch path
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a Home Assistant install with large attributes on a high-rate entity, which is not a typical single-user setup. `format_trigger_value` runs `json.dumps` on the whole value and only then cuts it to 255 characters. It runs for old and new, per listener per event. A large tracked attribute (a long `source_list`, an image-bearing attribute) on a fast-updating entity pays the full serialization cost on every run to store 255 characters. D2 bounded storage, not CPU.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: tracking a large, fast-changing attribute serializes the whole value on each run before it is cut to 255 characters.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: tracking a large, fast-changing attribute serializes the whole value on each run before it is cut to 255 characters.

findings.title: `hassette execution --json` can't tell "not found" from "lookup failed" on stdout
findings.why_it_matters: Both cases produce `{"execution": null, "logs": [...]}` and exit 0. The only difference is a stderr warning. A script or Claude-driven troubleshooting that reads only stdout, which is D6's stated consumer, can't distinguish "retry in a few seconds" from "the telemetry endpoint is broken". D6 ratified this leniency. The open question is whether the document should carry the reason, since #3677 will add keys to this object anyway.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: in `--json`, a failed execution lookup and a missing record both read `"execution": null`; the failure reason is on stderr only.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: in `--json`, a failed execution lookup and a missing record both read `"execution": null`; the failure reason is on stderr only.

findings.title: Pre-023 handler rows get a non-null `trigger` object with every field None
findings.why_it_matters: `execution_from_row` builds an `ExecutionTrigger` for every handler row, including old rows that have neither context nor topic. The behaviour is documented ("None for jobs, set on every handler row"), but a consumer can't use `trigger is None` to mean "no trigger recorded", and `if execution.trigger:` is True for an empty object because a Pydantic model is truthy. The frontend guards on `trigger?.context_id` and is fine.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a pre-023 handler row's `trigger` is an object with every field None, so consumers check fields rather than the object.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a pre-023 handler row's `trigger` is an object with every field None, so consumers check fields rather than the object.

findings.title: `summarize_trigger` says "never raises", but the pre-`try` reads can raise in the predicate-failure path
Synthetic rows reuse a historical context id, so `trigger_context_id` stops identifying one event
Extraction-failure log includes exception text that can embed the value
The released-client break is silent, and the compat check can't detect it
